summary.text: Letting \(k=\lfloor rn\rfloor\), \(x=\{rn\}\), and \(c=r-2\), the identities \(r^2=2r+\tfrac14\) and \(rk=2k+\tfrac n4-cx\), together with irrationality of \(rn\), give \(0<x<1\) and \(0<c<\tfrac14\). Splitting on \(j=n\bmod 4\), the error simplifies to \(1+2x\) when \(j=0\), and to \(\tfrac j4+2x\) when \(j=1,2,3\), from which the strict bounds follow immediately.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
r=\frac{2+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad a(n)=\left\lfloor r\left\lfloor rn\right\rfloor\right\rfloor.
\]
We prove that for every integer \(n\ge 1\),
\[
\frac14<nr^2-a(n)<3.
\]

For a real number \(t\), write
\[
\{t\}=t-\lfloor t\rfloor
\]
for its fractional part. Thus \(0\le \{t\}<1\), and adding an integer does not change the fractional part.

First record two facts about \(r\). Since
\[
2<\sqrt5<\frac52
\]
(the inequalities follow by squaring, since \(4<5<25/4\)), if we put
\[
c=r-2=\frac{\sqrt5-2}{2},
\]
then
\[
0<c<\frac14. \tag{1}
\]
Also,
\[
r^2=2r+\frac14. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, using \((\sqrt5)^2=5\),
\[
r^2=\left(\frac{2+\sqrt5}{2}\right)^2
=\frac{4+4\sqrt5+5}{4}
=\frac94+\sqrt5
=2\left(\frac{2+\sqrt5}{2}\right)+\frac14.
\]

Fix an integer \(n\ge1\), and define
\[
k=\lfloor rn\rfloor,\qquad x=\{rn\}.
\]
Then
\[
rn=k+x. \tag{3}
\]
In fact the inequalities for the fractional part are strict at the lower end here:
\[
0<x<1. \tag{4}
\]
The upper bound is the general property of fractional parts. For the lower bound, \(\sqrt5\) is irrational: if \(\sqrt5=p/q\) in lowest terms, then \(p^2=5q^2\); primality of \(5\) implies \(5\mid p\), and substituting \(p=5t\) then implies \(5\mid q\), contradicting that \(p/q\) was reduced. Consequently \(r=(2+\sqrt5)/2\) is irrational. Since \(n\ne0\), \(rn\) is irrational as well (otherwise division by the nonzero integer \(n\) would make \(r\) rational). Hence \(rn\) is not an integer, so its fractional part is not zero. This proves (4).

Because \(r>2\) and \(n\ge1\), the quantities involved in the nested floor are nonnegative, so the natural-number interpretation of \(a(n)\) agrees with the ordinary integer floor \(\lfloor rk\rfloor\). From (3),
\[
nr^2=r(rn)=r(k+x)=rk+rx.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
nr^2-a(n)
&=rk+rx-\lfloor rk\rfloor\\
&=\{rk\}+rx. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus it remains to calculate the fractional part of \(rk\).

Using (3), we have \(k=nr-x\). Therefore, by (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
rk
&=r(nr-x)\\
&=nr^2-rx\\
&=n\left(2r+\frac14\right)-rx\\
&=2nr+\frac n4-rx\\
&=2(k+x)+\frac n4-rx\\
&=2k+\frac n4-(r-2)x\\
&=2k+\frac n4-cx. \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
The term \(2k\) is an integer and hence does not affect a fractional part. Write the Euclidean division of \(n\) by \(4\) as
\[
n=4q+j,
\]
where \(q\) is an integer and
\[
j\in\{0,1,2,3\}.
\]
Then \(n/4=q+j/4\), and the integer term \(q\) also does not affect a fractional part. Equation (6) consequently gives
\[
\{rk\}=\left\{\frac j4-cx\right\}. \tag{7}
\]

By (1) and (4),
\[
0<cx<\frac14. \tag{8}
\]
We now evaluate (7), splitting into the four possible values of \(j\).

* If \(j=0\), then \(-1<-cx<0\), so
  \[
  \left\{-cx\right\}=1-cx.
  \]

* If \(j=1\), then (8) gives
  \[
  0<\frac14-cx<1,
  \]
  so its fractional part is itself:
  \[
  \left\{\frac14-cx\right\}=\frac14-cx.
  \]

* If \(j=2\), then
  \[
  0<\frac12-cx<1,
  \]
  and hence
  \[
  \left\{\frac12-cx\right\}=\frac12-cx.
  \]

* If \(j=3\), then
  \[
  0<\frac34-cx<1,
  \]
  and hence
  \[
  \left\{\frac34-cx\right\}=\frac34-cx.
  \]

Since \(r=c+2\), substituting these four evaluations into (5) causes the terms involving \(c\) to cancel. Explicitly,
\[
nr^2-a(n)=
\begin{cases}
(1-cx)+(c+2)x=1+2x, & j=0,\\[2mm]
(\frac14-cx)+(c+2)x=\frac14+2x, & j=1,\\[2mm]
(\frac12-cx)+(c+2)x=\frac12+2x, & j=2,\\[2mm]
(\frac34-cx)+(c+2)x=\frac34+2x, & j=3.
\end{cases} \tag{9}
\]

Finally use \(0<x<1\). In the four cases, (9) respectively yields
\[
1<1+2x<3,
\]
\[
\frac14<\frac14+2x<\frac94<3,
\]
\[
\frac12<\frac12+2x<\frac52<3,
\]
and
\[
\frac34<\frac34+2x<\frac{11}{4}<3.
\]
Every case therefore satisfies
\[
\frac14<nr^2-a(n)<3.
\]
This proves the assertion for every integer \(n\ge1\).
